content: Viral hepatitis encompasses several types of liver infections caused by different viruses, including hepatitis A, B, C, D, and E. Each type has unique characteristics, modes of transmission, prevention strategies, and treatment options. Hepatitis A is a liver infection caused by the hepatitis A virus (HAV). It is primarily spread through the ingestion of contaminated food or water or close contact with an infected person. Symptoms may include fatigue, nausea, abdominal pain, jaundice, and dark urine. Vaccination is the most effective way to prevent hepatitis A, and treatment focuses on supportive care as the infection typically resolves on its own. Hepatitis B is caused by the hepatitis B virus (HBV) and is transmitted through contact with infected blood, semen, or other bodily fluids. It can lead to both acute and chronic liver disease. Symptoms may include fever, fatigue, loss of appetite, nausea, jaundice, and joint pain. Vaccination is highly effective in preventing hepatitis B, and antiviral medications are available for managing chronic infections. Hepatitis C is caused by the hepatitis C virus (HCV) and is primarily spread through blood-to-blood contact, such as sharing needles or receiving contaminated blood products. Many individuals with hepatitis C are asymptomatic, but chronic infection can lead to severe liver damage, including cirrhosis and liver cancer. Testing is essential for diagnosis, and direct-acting antiviral medications can cure most cases of hepatitis C. Hepatitis D, also known as delta hepatitis, is caused by the hepatitis D virus (HDV) and only occurs in individuals already infected with hepatitis B. It is transmitted through contact with infected blood or bodily fluids. Symptoms and complications are similar to those of hepatitis B but are often more severe. Prevention relies on hepatitis B vaccination, as there is no specific vaccine for hepatitis D. Treatment options are limited and may include antiviral therapies. Hepatitis E is caused by the hepatitis E virus (HEV) and is typically transmitted through the consumption of contaminated water. It is more common in developing countries with poor sanitation. Symptoms include fever, fatigue, nausea, jaundice, and abdominal pain. The infection is usually self-limiting, but it can be severe in pregnant women. Prevention focuses on improving sanitation and access to clean water. The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) collaborates with partners to investigate and respond to viral hepatitis outbreaks. Surveillance systems are in place to monitor trends, analyze data, and guide public health interventions. The CDC also provides resources and guidance for state and local health departments to improve case management and prevention efforts. The Division of Viral Hepatitis (DVH) within the CDC is dedicated to eliminating viral hepatitis as a public health threat. This includes raising awareness through initiatives like Hepatitis Awareness Month in May and Hepatitis Testing Day on May 19. The DVH also supports global efforts, such as World Hepatitis Day on July 28, to highlight the global burden of viral hepatitis and promote prevention, testing, and treatment. Specific populations, including healthcare professionals and individuals at increased risk, are a focus of targeted interventions to reduce the impact of viral hepatitis. The CDC emphasizes the importance of vaccination, testing, and early treatment to prevent complications and improve outcomes. The CDC also defines influential scientific information through peer-reviewed research to guide evidence-based policies and programs. Funded partners and programs play a critical role in advancing the goals of the Division of Viral Hepatitis and addressing the needs of affected communities.
